candidate.blueprint_locator: Printed p.13, Reduction of Risk Potential — review laboratory results and recognize complications/risk patterns
candidate.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — DIC laboratory interpretation
candidate.educational_objective: Avoid excluding DIC on the basis of one normal fibrinogen result; interpret fibrinogen as one component of the clinical and laboratory pattern used to evaluate suspected DIC.

options.A: A normal fibrinogen result by itself rules out DIC.
options.B: DIC can be diagnosed only when fibrinogen is below the reference interval.
options.C: A normal fibrinogen result alone does not rule out DIC; the diagnosis depends on the clinical setting and the overall coagulation pattern, including platelet count, PT/aPTT, fibrin-related markers, and fibrinogen.
options.D: Fibrinogen has no role in evaluating suspected DIC.

candidate.rationale: NCBI StatPearls states that no single history, examination, or laboratory component can diagnose or rule out DIC. Evaluation uses the clinical context together with a pattern of laboratory findings such as platelet count, PT/aPTT, fibrin-related markers, and fibrinogen. A decreased fibrinogen level can support DIC, but a fibrinogen result within the reference interval cannot by itself exclude the diagnosis. C is therefore the most accurate interpretation.
candidate.source_claim_supported: No single laboratory component, including fibrinogen, can rule out DIC; evaluation requires the clinical setting and a pattern of coagulation findings.
candidate.source_locator: Evaluation — no single history, physical examination, or laboratory component can diagnose or rule out DIC; laboratory pattern includes PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, platelet count, schistocytes, and fibrin-related markers

candidate.stem: A client with a clinical condition associated with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) has a fibrinogen result within the laboratory reference interval. Which interpretation is most accurate?
